subsection: 3. Developing, evaluating and improving a marketing mix; the USP

notes.h: What a unique selling point is
notes.b: Customers choose between rival offers, so a business needs something that makes its own offer stand out. That standout feature or benefit is its unique selling point (USP), and it is one source of competitive advantage (any edge that lets a business win customers from rivals).
points: A unique selling point is the feature or benefit that sets a product or service apart from competitors and gives customers a reason to choose it.
A USP must be something customers value, which is why the target market (the group of customers the business aims at) matters: a feature no one wants is not a useful USP.

A strong USP is distinctive, relevant to the target market and difficult for competitors to imitate quickly. It is unique relative to competitors at a point in time, and many USPs can be copied, which is why defensibility is analysed.

A USP can come from price, quality, convenience, speed, origin, design, service, sustainability or branding. For example, a firm might stand out because it delivers faster or because its ingredients come from a named place.
A USP is not the same as a slogan: the slogan communicates the USP, but the USP itself must be grounded in what the offer actually delivers.
notes.tip: A common mistake is confusing a slogan with a USP. The slogan is how the USP is communicated; the USP is the real benefit the customer receives.

notes.b: A USP analysis tests a claimed advantage against three questions before the business builds its marketing around it. Analysing means studying the advantage in detail and bringing out its essential elements.
points: Uniqueness: identify exactly what is different about the offer and check it against the main competitors' offers, because a feature rivals already match is not unique.

Customer value: confirm that the difference matters to the target market, for example by testing it in market research such as a survey or field research, because a difference customers ignore will not win sales.

Defensibility: assess whether competitors could copy the feature, price or service quickly, and what barriers protect it. A patent (a legal right giving an inventor exclusive use of an invention for a set period) or strong brand loyalty are examples.
Conclusion: a USP that is unique and valued but easily copied needs supporting advantages, such as strong service or brand reputation, to hold its position.
A USP claim is only as strong as its evidence. An unsupported claim becomes a liability, because customers who find it untrue lose trust in the business.
notes.tip: A full USP analysis tests uniqueness, customer value and defensibility and then reaches a conclusion. A common mistake is ignoring defensibility.

notes.h: Developing a 7-P marketing mix for a product: a sample porridge-pot business
notes.b: The marketing mix is the seven Ps (product, pricing, promotion, people, packaging, process and place), and each P is shaped by the target market. This worked mix is for a sample porridge-pot business, an illustrative example rather than a real firm, selling a premium ready-to-eat porridge pot made from traceable Irish oats to busy adults who want a healthy breakfast.
points: Product: a single-serve porridge pot in three flavours, with no added sugar and a clear list of ingredients, because busy adults want a quick breakfast they can trust to be healthy.
Pricing: premium pricing (a price set above mainstream porridge pots), justified by the traceable sourcing and quality of the oats, which the target market values.

Promotion: social media posts that show the farms the oats come from, tasting events at Irish gyms and cafes, and sponsorship of a local running club. These reach health-minded adults where they already spend time.
People: a small team of brand ambassadors who run tastings at farmers' markets and answer questions about sourcing with confidence, so the sourcing claim is backed by knowledgeable staff.
Packaging: a recyclable cardboard sleeve with a tear-off lid, labelled with ingredients, allergens and the named farm of origin, which supports both the healthy image and the sustainability message.
Process: online pre-orders for weekly delivery to offices by a local courier, with reminders sent before each delivery, so ordering is easy for busy customers.
Place: sold through independent Irish grocers and cafes, plus the brand's own website, combining indirect channels (through a retailer) and a direct channel (straight to the customer).
Other products follow the same steps: choose a target market, then make a consistent decision for each of the seven Ps and tie it to that market.
notes.tip: A full answer covers all seven Ps, ties each to the target market and keeps them consistent. A common mistake is missing people, packaging or process, or adding physical evidence as an extra P.

notes.h: USP analysis for the porridge pot
notes.b: The porridge pot's claimed advantage is traceable Irish oats from named farms. Applying the three tests shows how strong that claim is.
points: Uniqueness: most mainstream porridge pots state Irish origin in general terms, while this business names the farms that supply each batch.
Customer value: busy adults who care about local food and transparency are willing to pay a premium for a verifiable origin, which is why the premium price in the mix is workable.
Defensibility: competitors can claim Irish origin, but naming farms and publishing verifiable supply contracts is harder to copy quickly.

Weakness: the claim is only as strong as its evidence, so the business must keep supply records accurate or the USP becomes a liability. A false origin claim could also be a misleading practice under the Consumer Protection Act 2007.
notes.tip: State the conclusion as well as the three tests. Here the USP is defensible only if the supply records are accurate.

notes.h: Developing a 7-P marketing mix for a service: a sample mobile bike-repair service in Galway
notes.b: For a service, people, process and packaging weigh more heavily than for a physical good, because the customer experiences the service being delivered. This worked mix is for a sample mobile bike-repair service in Galway, an illustrative example rather than a real firm, which visits customers' homes and offices.
points: Service: mobile servicing and repair of bicycles at the customer's door, including safety checks, tune-ups, puncture repair and brake and gear adjustment.

Pricing: fixed prices for standard jobs shown online, set slightly above a workshop's rates to reflect convenience, with a volume discount for corporate contracts. Fixed prices let customers know the cost before booking.

Promotion: local social media and search advertising, referrals from cycling clubs and a partnership with employers' wellbeing schemes, which reach the commuters and office workers the service targets.
People: qualified mechanics trained in customer service, who explain the work and the price before starting any job, because customers cannot inspect a service in advance and rely on the mechanic.
Packaging: a service has no box, so here packaging is applied as the presentation of the service. The business uses a branded van, a printed job card and a clean finish on every bike.

Process: online booking for a chosen time slot, a reminder message before the visit, a job card recording the work done and card payment on completion. Process matters especially for a service because the steps are the product.
Place: the van travels to the customer, so the service is delivered where the customer is, and the base workshop is used only for parts and storage.
Any other service follows the same steps: the seven Ps stay the same, with each decision tied to the target market.
notes.tip: Choose your own service in the exam and use these steps. A common mistake is leaving out people, packaging or process, or adding physical evidence as an extra P.

notes.h: USP analysis for the bike-repair service
notes.b: The service's claimed advantage is that it comes to the customer. The analysis tests whether this advantage can be sustained.
points: Uniqueness: the business repairs bikes at the customer's door, so the customer does not lose time travelling to a shop or carrying the bike.
Customer value: commuters and busy families value the saved time and are willing to pay for it, which supports the slightly higher price.
Defensibility: a competitor might offer collection, so the advantage can be copied. The business must build a reputation for speed and reliability, a supporting advantage, to hold it.
Suggested extension: a same-day service would strengthen the proposition, though it would need more mechanics and a tighter route plan, which adds cost.
notes.tip: A full analysis ends with a conclusion and, where the USP is easy to copy, a supporting advantage or extension.

notes.h: Recommending a launch strategy from a firm's advantage
notes.b: A launch strategy applies the USP to the mix. The approach is to identify the advantage and then use it to make marketing decisions.
points: Identify the competitive advantage from the stimulus (the information given in the question) and link it to what the customer gains. For example, traceable oats give health-minded customers confidence in the origin.

Recommend a pricing choice that uses the advantage, with a reason. A premium price fits an advantage customers value, while penetration pricing (a low price to win customers quickly) suits a new entrant.
Recommend a promotion choice that communicates the advantage to the target market, such as social media that shows the farms or the convenience of the service.
Recommend a place choice that reaches the target market, such as independent grocers and an own website, or a van that travels to the customer, and give the reason each choice suits the advantage.
notes.tip: Identify means state the advantage briefly, taken from the stimulus. A common mistake is listing features the stimulus does not show, or listing the Ps with no link to the advantage.

notes.b: A marketing mix is evaluated against five criteria to see whether it serves the target market and supports profit. To evaluate is to judge with evidence, so each criterion needs a strength, a weakness and a reason.
points: Fit with the target market: each P should match the needs, budget and media habits of the customers it aims to reach.
Consistency between the Ps: a premium price combined with heavy discounting sends mixed signals and weakens the brand.
Competitiveness: the mix should give customers a reason to choose the business over rivals, built on its USP.
Profitability: revenue must exceed the costs of the mix, including promotion, packaging and delivery.

Ethics and sustainability: the mix should avoid misleading claims and wasteful packaging, because these damage trust over time. Recyclable packaging or local sourcing can be a USP, but it can also add cost, so judge it honestly.
Method: judge each criterion with evidence from the business, state strengths and weaknesses, then reach a justified overall judgement.
notes.tip: Apply at least three criteria, give a strength and a weakness for each, and finish with an overall judgement. A common mistake is describing the mix without judging it. Do not confuse this with a USP analysis, which tests only one advantage.

notes.b: Improving a mix means changing it. The evaluation shows the weakest element or the mismatch between the mix and the target market, and the improvement is aimed there.
points: Pricing: when sales are weak against cheaper rivals, a bundle or an introductory offer can widen the appeal without cutting the core price.
Promotion: spending can move to the channels the target market actually uses, with results measured through response rates, so money is not wasted on channels the customers ignore.

Process: slow or manual steps, such as phone-only booking, can be replaced with online ordering to save time for both sides. Digital tools like this are common improvements, but they also make a USP easier to copy.
Packaging: a design that looks dated, or that customers see as wasteful, can be refreshed with lighter or more recyclable materials.
People: when customers report poor experiences, training and clearer service standards address the cause, since service depends on staff.
Match the improvement to the weakest element. Name the P, the specific change and the effect it should have.
notes.tip: A common mistake is a vague 'improve advertising'. A full answer names the weakest P, a specific change and its expected effect.

notes.b: A marketing mix is modified as the product moves through its life cycle (introduction, growth, maturity and decline) and as customers, competitors and costs change. This differs from improving a mix, which fixes a weakness found in an evaluation.
points: In the introduction stage the mix emphasises awareness and may use penetration pricing (a low price to win customers quickly) and heavy promotion, because few customers know the product yet.
In growth the business widens distribution and builds the brand, so more customers can buy the product and recognise it.
In maturity the mix often shifts towards loyalty, price competition and cost control, because sales growth has levelled off and rivals compete hard.
In decline the business may reduce spending and drop weak channels, or it may reposition the product for a new group of customers.
Competitor moves, new technology, such as online ordering, and changing costs can force changes to place and process at any stage.
notes.tip: Keep the three terms apart: evaluating judges the mix, improving changes a weak element, and modifying changes the mix over time as the life cycle and market change.

keyTerms.definition: The distinctive feature or benefit that sets a product or service apart from competitors and gives customers a reason to choose it.
Testing a claimed advantage for its uniqueness, its value to customers and whether competitors could copy it.
The extent to which a competitive advantage can be protected from being copied by rivals.
A legal right that gives an inventor exclusive use of an invention for a set period of time.
Repeat buying and commitment to a brand that make customers less likely to switch to competitors.
The extent to which all elements of the marketing mix send the same message about the brand and its target market.
Changing the elements of the mix as a product moves through its life cycle or as market conditions change.
The amount added to the cost of a product to set its selling price, usually expressed as a proportion of that cost.

factCards.term: Five criteria for evaluating a mix
factCards.definition: Fit with the target market, consistency, competitiveness, profitability, and ethics and sustainability.
Adjusting price, redirecting promotion, streamlining the process, refreshing packaging and training staff.

factCards.term: How the mix changes by stage
factCards.definition: Introduction emphasises awareness; maturity emphasises loyalty and cost control; decline may reposition the product or reduce spending.
A slogan or a vague claim such as quality is not a USP unless the offer actually delivers it in a way customers can see.

questions.prompt: Develop a full 7-P marketing mix for a product of your choice, and carry out a USP analysis for the product.
questions.model: Consider a reusable steel water bottle sold to students and office workers in Cork. Product: a durable bottle with a leak-proof lid, in a range of colours, with a warranty and a replacement lid service. Pricing: a mid-premium price, set above supermarket bottles to reflect durability, with a bundle offer for students. Promotion: social media and campus ambassadors who show the bottle in daily use, plus partnerships with cafes that offer a discount to customers who refill. People: staff trained to explain the warranty and the refill scheme. Packaging: recycled card packaging with a clear care guide, since the product is sold on sustainability. Process: online ordering with a simple returns process and fast delivery to student accommodation. Place: sold online, through campus shops and in selected sports stores. USP analysis: the uniqueness lies in the lifetime warranty and replacement lid service, which few rivals offer. Customer value is high, because students who replace cheap bottles often value a product that lasts. Defensibility is moderate: rivals can copy a warranty, but the firm can strengthen its position through the refill scheme and the brand's sustainability record.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the marketing mix of a service business whose bookings are falling, and suggest two ways of improving it.
questions.model: Evaluation: the mix may fail the fit test if its promotion still reaches customers through channels they have stopped using, such as print advertising, while the target market now books online. The process may also be weak if booking requires a phone call, which deters younger customers. Consistency matters too: if the price is premium but the promotion uses frequent discounts, the message is confused. Improvement one: move promotion to social media and search advertising, measuring response rates, so spending is directed at the channels the target market uses. Improvement two: streamline the process by adding online booking with reminders, which saves time for customers and reduces missed appointments. Both changes address the weakest elements of the mix while keeping the price and brand intact.
